rejected.title: Correlation and causation
card: A correlation is when two things change together. When one goes up, the other tends to go up too, or tends to go down.
A correlation does not prove that one thing causes the other. The link may be a coincidence.
A third factor may cause both changes. In summer, hot weather can raise both ice cream sales and the number of people swimming at a beach.
To show that one thing causes another, scientists need more evidence, such as a fair test that changes only that one thing.
rejected.remember: Changing together is a correlation. It is not proof of cause.

a.q: In one town, months with more ice cream sales also have more sunburn cases. What can be concluded from this data alone?
opts: They are correlated, but this alone does not show a cause
They are correlated, which shows ice cream causes sunburn
They are correlated, which proves sunburn boosts sales
They are not linked, because neither one causes the other
a.why: Sales and sunburn rise together, so they are correlated, but a correlation alone cannot prove cause. A third factor such as hot sunny weather could explain both. Saying ice cream causes sunburn is tempting, but it reads cause into a pattern that does not show it.
a.clue: Does changing together prove that one thing causes the other?

b.q: A survey finds that students who own more books score higher in science tests. Which statement is best supported by this survey alone?
opts: Book ownership and test scores are correlated
Buying more books raises a student's test score
High test scores make students buy more books
Book ownership and test scores have no link at all
b.why: The survey shows the two change together, which is a correlation. It does not show that books cause higher scores, as a third factor such as time spent reading may explain both. The survey does not show that there is no link either, since the two do move together.
b.clue: The survey shows a pattern but did not run a fair test.
